title: pgo-tokenizer-ffi-thaw-policy-retrospective
content:
Summary:

This doc captures a focused investigation we ran in Q2 2025 into a persistent CPU-side latency tail for small requests (payload <= 512B). The goal was to reduce p95/p99 across the hosted API without impacting throughput for large batches. We experimented with three levers in parallel: 1) PGO-guided tokenizer micro-optimizations, 2) an FFI batching shim to reduce Python->C crossing overhead for short-lived tokenization calls, and 3) a conservative thread thaw/unpark policy for the request worker pool to reduce wakeup thrash.

Why this matterd (motivation):
- Small requests are ~60% of our traffic for chat-preview and quick-embed endpoints; their tail dominates user-visible latency when we autoscale down.
- Previous sampling pointed to ~40-60% of CPU time spent in tokenization-related C code + Python wrapper overhead for these requests.
- Ephemeral worker park/unpark churn amplified tail during short bursts (hundreds of req/s) after idle periods.

Hypotheses tested:
1) Using PGO profiles from production traces to drive small-code hot-path layout and branch prediction will reduce instruction cache misses and branch mispredicts inside the tokenizer hot loop, lowering CPU cycles per token.
2) Coalescing multiple short tokenization requests inside a single FFI call reduces per-request crossing overhead and GIL knife-edge contention, improving p95 without increasing single-request latency beyond +/- 5%.
3) Adding a short thaw-delay (8ms) and exponential backoff for unparking workers reduces syscalls/context-switch rate and helps tail latency during bursty workloads.

Experiment matrix and setup:
- Baseline: current mainline runtime (no PGO, per-request C-extension call, default threadpool park/unpark).
- PGO tokenizer build: collect production-like traffic (staging traces) with perf, generate profile, recompile tokenizer C-extension with -fprofile-generate / -fprofile-use and cache-aware function layout.
- FFI-batching shim: an opt-in Python C-extension API token_batchize(bufs: List[bytes]) -> List[token arrays]; implemented minimal copy strategy (shared read-only slab per batch) to keep memory cost low.
- Thaw policy: introduce config thaw_delay_ms (default 0 -> existing behavior) and experiment with 4ms/8ms/16ms. Implemented in threadpool park/unpark path in runtime worker manager.
- Workload: synthetic replay of live sampling for small-req-heavy routes (1k rps sustained, 10s bursts up to 6k rps), real-model inference stubbed to isolate preproc + serving warmup behavior.
- Tools: perf record/top, bpftrace for syscall tracing, py-spy for Python stack sampling, flamegraph generation, custom microprofiler counters (per-request: ms tokenization, crossing overhead, park/unpark count).

Key measurements (representative):
- Baseline small-request p50/p95/p99: 4.6ms / 18.2ms / 37.9ms
- After PGO-tokenizer only: 4.4ms / 14.9ms / 32.1ms  (p95 -18%, p99 -15%)
- After FFI-batching only: 4.7ms / 12.6ms / 25.8ms (p95 -31%, p99 -32%)
- PGO + FFI combined: 4.3ms / 11.8ms / 23.4ms  (best single run)
- Thaw policy (8ms) applied to combined: p50/p95/p99: 4.5ms / 10.9ms / 20.8ms (p99 -45% vs baseline)
- CPU util change: combined changes reduced avg CPU cycles per request by ~22% for small requests.
- Syscalls/context-switches: FFI-batching reduced frequent short syscalls (write/recvmsg/unix-domain) count by ~40% during bursts; thaw policy reduced park/unpark syscall rate by ~55% during burst recovery.

Qualitative observations from traces/flamegraphs:
- Baseline flamegraphs often showed a thin but tall stack of Python wrapper -> C tokenization entry -> repeated small allocations and immediate free. The wrapper overhead plus per-call GIL grab/ungrab accounted for ~35% of wall time in hot traces.
- PGO build reduced the hot loop branch mispredict tail and improved instruction-cache locality; perf stat showed branch-misses down ~28% in optimized build.
- FFI batching aggregated many tiny Python->C transitions into a single higher-latency call but with net savings: reduced GIL churn and amortized small allocations. We saw a modest increase in peak resident set during large-batch scenarios but within capacity. Memory bump ~3-6MB per worker for sampled runs.
- Thaw policy tradeoff: introducing an 8ms thaw delay increased median slightly for perfectly steady load (1-2ms) but dramatically reduced tail during bursty start/stop patterns, because it prevented a tight park/unpark loop when request inter-arrival jumps around the wake threshold.

Corner cases and regressions observed:
- Some legacy customers that rely on per-request tokenization side-effects (rare) observed subtle behavioral differences with FFI-batching because we normalized ephemeral buffer lifetimes; we added a compatibility flag to preserve old semantics.
- In very high throughput large-batch runs (truly large requests), FFI-batching produced no improvement and slightly increased some microbenchmarks due to extra copy amortization; we gate FFI-batching to only opt-in for small request paths.
- PGO build increased CI time and required staging traffic capture. We added a reproducible profile generation job that runs nightly on representative sample traces to reduce drift.

Actionable next steps (short term):
1) Ship FFI-batching as opt-in behind a feature flag and enable by default for small-request routes in hosted API (rollout via canary 5% -> 25% -> 100%). See PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2893.
2) Merge PGO-tokenizer build pipeline into release build; add profile collection job and fallback when profile not present. Track CI time and build cache improvements.
3) Set default thaw_delay_ms = 8ms for worker manager, with knobs per pool; expose in Dedicated/Private runtime config as runtime tuning parameter.
4) Instrument longer-term metrics: per-route tokenization cycles/request, aggregate GIL-hold time per request, park/unpark syscall rate, and memory delta when FFI-batching enabled. Add dashboard panels under "serving-runtime/tokenization".
5) Post-rollout, schedule a week-long A/B test comparing error rates and quality (some small changes in tokenization order with batching required QA to ensure no regression).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Can we apply similar PGO-guided layout to parser/JSON path to reduce request-parse tail? Early perf indicates some wins but needs independent profile sets.
- Is there a hybrid mode where we dynamically choose per-request whether to use FFI-batch based on payload size and current memory pressure? Prototype idea: fast-path if len(payload) < 512B and worker mem usage < threshold.
- Investigate whether futex wakeups could be further reduced by switching to an M:N worker model for tiny requests; requires larger design work.

Appendix: commands and profiling notes (how we reproduced)
- Capture profile for PGO:
  perf record -F 99 -g -p $(pidof runtime) -o /tmp/prof.data -- sleep 60
  perf script -i /tmp/prof.data | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > tokenizer-baseline.svg
- Microbench tokenization crossing overhead:
  python tools/tokenize_microbench.py --rps 1000 --workers 8 --size 256 --runs 10
- bpftrace syscall rate (park/unpark focused):
  bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_futex { @[comm] = count(); } interval:s:1 { print(@); clear(@); }'
- py-spy sampling on worker thread during bursts:
  py-spy record -o pyspy.svg --pid $(pidof runtime) --native --duration 30

Notes to reviewers:
- The raw perf logs and flamegraphs are uploaded to the profiling bucket (link in Confluence page above).
- PR #2893 contains the FFI shim and a compatibility opt-out. Please review for safety and memory edge cases.
- If we proceed, product should be notified because some customers might observe tiny changes in tokenization timing; we plan to run the QA tokenset regression harness before reaching 100% rollout.

Personal takeaway: small wins compound. PGO gave consistent base improvement but the asymmetric benefit came from reducing boundary crossings and OS-level wakeup noise. The thaw-policy was the low-risk, high-impact change for our tail behavior during real burst patterns.

-- Ava
